Summarise the net benefit of a model

summary.voipred_nb.Rd

print() shows the net benefit at the first thresholds; summary() adds the best strategy at each threshold, the largest gain of each model, and the models' sensitivity and specificity; as.data.frame() returns the estimates at every threshold.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'voipred_nb'
print(x, n = 10, per = getOption("voipred.per", 1), ...)

# S3 method for class 'voipred_nb'
summary(
  object,
  thresholds = NULL,
  per = getOption("voipred.per", 1),
  comparator = "Treat All",
  k = NULL,
  shares = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'voipred_nb'
as.data.frame(
  x,
  row.names = NULL,
  optional = FALSE,
  per = getOption("voipred.per", 1),
  ...
)

Arguments

n

Number of thresholds printed. Default 10.

per

Scale of the net benefit: the number of patients it is expressed per. Default 1 (per patient, the usual scale); e.g. per = 100000 gives the net number of true positives per 100,000 patients. print() and summary() show NB_model, NB_all, NB_none and delta_NB on that scale (the header says so); as.data.frame() keeps the per-patient columns and adds the scaled ones, named <column>_per_<per> (e.g. NB_model_per_100000). The result itself is always per patient. The default can be set once with options(voipred.per = 100000).

...

Not used.

object, x

A result of nb_val().

thresholds

Optional thresholds to show in the table (among those of the result); default: all, of which the first 10 are printed.

comparator, k, shares

For a result with subgroups (nb_val(subgroup = ), see "Subgroups" in nb_val()): the comparator of the subgroup differences in net benefit, "Treat All" (default), "Treat None", "best default" (treat all or treat none, whichever is better in the whole sample at the threshold) or another model; k, the incremental utility of a true positive relative to a false negative (\(a - c\)) in each subgroup, e.g. the relative risk reduction of the treatment: values named by subgroup, e.g. c(male = 0.28, female = 0.15), or (any number of subgroups) ranges, e.g. list(male = c(0.2, 0.3), ...); shares, the relative sizes of the subgroups in the target population (default: in the sample). summary() then adds the checks of Wang et al.: the subgroup differences in net benefit against the comparator (diff_NB_<subgroup>; distinct from delta_NB, which is against the best default strategy of each group), their share-weighted sum (diff_NB_population), whether they have the same sign, the K-value (two subgroups) and, with k, the utility-weighted difference (diff_utility) and whether population net benefit and population utility favour the same strategy (consistent).

row.names, optional

Not used (as in as.data.frame()).

Value

summary(): an object of class summary.voipred_nb, printed as shown: the best strategy at each threshold, the largest delta_NB of each model, and the table (columns threshold, model, Se, Sp, NB_model, NB_all, NB_none, delta_NB). as.data.frame(): the estimates data frame (columns threshold, model, NB_model, NB_all, NB_none, delta_NB).

Details

All three have the same layout, for one model or several: one row per threshold and model, the model's label in the column model, and the columns NB_model, NB_all, NB_none and delta_NB (summary() adds Se and Sp). print() and summary() sort the rows by threshold, so that the models are side by side; as.data.frame() keeps the order of the estimates (by model, then threshold).

With credible intervals (nb_val(interval = )), print() and summary() show the interval of NB_model and of delta_NB after each of them, e.g. 95% CrI (0.0208, 0.0596), the header says how they were computed, and as.data.frame() has the bounds (NB_model_lower, NB_model_upper, ...); plot(bands = TRUE) draws them as bands.

The best strategy at a threshold is the model with the largest delta_NB if it is positive, otherwise treat all if its net benefit is positive, otherwise treat none. For a binary outcome, sensitivity and specificity are posterior means (the observed proportions with the default improper prior). For survival and competing-risks outcomes they are those of the event by the horizon, from the same estimates as the net benefit: with Kaplan-Meier, from the Kaplan-Meier (Aalen-Johansen) risk by the horizon \(F\), the share treated \(q\) and the risk among the treated \(F_+\), \(Se = q F_+ / F\) and \(Sp = 1 - q (1 - F_+) / (1 - F)\); with cIPCW (cipcw), the IPCW-weighted proportions of the cIPCW estimator.

See also

nb_val(), plot.voipred_nb()

Examples

df_dev_binary <- gusto[1:5000, ]
df_val_binary <- gusto[5001:5500, ]
fit <- glm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse,
           family = binomial, data = df_dev_binary)
df_val_binary$p <- predict(fit, newdata = df_val_binary, type = "response")
res <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary,
              predicted_risk = df_val_binary$p,
              outcome = "day30",
              thresholds = seq(0.01, 0.3, by = 0.01))
res
#> Net benefit of p: binary, n = 500, 8 events (1.6%), prior improper Beta(0, 0)
#> 
#>  threshold model  NB_model   NB_all NB_none  delta_NB

#>       0.02     p  0.002041 -0.00408       0  0.002041
#>       0.03     p  0.000763 -0.01443       0  0.000763
#>       0.04     p -0.000750 -0.02500       0 -0.000750
#>       0.05     p -0.000421 -0.03579       0 -0.000421
#>       0.06     p -0.000511 -0.04681       0 -0.000511
#>       0.07     p -0.000602 -0.05806       0 -0.000602
#>       0.08     p -0.000348 -0.06957       0 -0.000348
#>       0.09     p -0.000198 -0.08132       0 -0.000198
#>       0.10     p -0.000222 -0.09333       0 -0.000222
#> # 20 more thresholds; use summary() or as.data.frame()
summary(res)
#> Net benefit of p: binary, n = 500, 8 events (1.6%), prior improper Beta(0, 0)
#> Best strategy: treat all 0.01, p 0.02-0.03, treat none 0.04-0.30

summary(res, thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
